<header>The principle in this passage is subtle</header>

The principle in this passage is subtle

<margin>Feeding at the breast</margin>
Children feeding <gloss>nursing</gloss> at their dead mother's breast. After a short while, she blinks <gloss>flickers</gloss> as if alive. They all abandon her and
<margin>The eyes moving means the mother died yet her eyes moved</margin>
<margin>They thought the blinking of the eyes meant she had not yet left them</margin>
run away. She is no longer present, and she no longer resembles herself. That which they loved in their mother
<margin>The stiffening of the body means she no longer resembles herself</margin>
<margin>If the form is not worth loving, then it is not worthy of being loved</margin>
was not her physical form. They loved that which gave life to her form. Those who die in battle, for their
<margin>Those who die in battle have no martial spirit, thus they are not provided with a funeral fan</margin>
burial, one does not provide a fan <gloss>a funeral banner or screen</gloss>. For the shoes of a man who has had his feet cut off, there is no reason to cherish them. All of these have lost
<margin>War is based on martial spirit</margin>
<margin>Shoes are based on the foot</margin>
<margin>Another metaphor is provided: Choosing concubines requires no nail trimming or ear piercing in order to preserve the completeness of the form, that they may serve the highest gaze</margin>
their root. Those serving as the various consorts of the Son of Heaven do not trim their nails or pierce their ears. Those who take
<margin>They are not used for official labor, for fear of causing calluses on their hands and feet, which would hinder the joy of new marriage</margin>
wives are stopped outside and may not be employed again. Even if the form is complete, it is still sufficient to be oneself. And yet,
<margin>One whose form is complete is still sufficient to move others</margin>
<margin>Following the meaning below, this is another distinct idea</margin>

<meta>This passage is from the chapter "The Sign of Virtue Complete" (De Chong Fu). The reference to "Ri Chuan Tang" (Sun and River Hall) likely refers to the printing house or the specific commentary edition.</meta>

<summary>This passage explores the distinction between loving a physical form and the vital principle that animates it, using metaphors of nursing infants, fallen soldiers, and palace consorts to argue that true worth lies in the preservation of the essential nature rather than the external shell.</summary>
<keywords>Zhuangzi, De Chong Fu, physical form, vital principle, essence, detachment</keywords>
